original_interpretation: TSMC states that CoWoS-R uses a redistribution-layer (RDL) interposer of polymer and copper traces with a minimum 4 µm pitch (2 µm line/space) and has been in volume production since 2023.
evidence_found: "CoWoS®-R advanced packaging service achieves heterogeneous integration by using a redistribution layer (RDL) interposer ... having been in volume production since 2023. An RDL interposer is comprised of polymer and copper traces"; "An RDL interposer for routing, with a minimum 4μm pitch (i.e., 2μm line width/spacing)." (TSMC CoWoS page, CoWoS-R section)
notes: Re-opened TSMC 3DFabric CoWoS page. All elements match. reported_claim is right (TSMC product page).

original_interpretation: TSMC states its CoWoS platform has been in volume production since 2012 and recommends CoWoS-L or CoWoS-R for interposers larger than 3.3 times reticle size.
evidence_found: "CoWoS®-L or CoWoS®-R are recommended for larger than 3.3X-reticle interposer sizes." ... "Since entering volume production in 2012, the CoWoS® platform has continued to evolve" (TSMC CoWoS page, introduction)
notes: Both statements found verbatim. Page also says CoWoS-S goes up to 3.3X reticle (~2700mm2).

original_interpretation: Intel's 2025 10-K states that EMIB, its 2.5D silicon-bridge packaging, entered high-volume manufacturing in 2017.
evidence_found: "EMIB, which entered high‑volume manufacturing in 2017, supports high‑density 2.5D integration" (Intel 10-K for FY ended 27 Dec 2025, Our Business - Packaging Technology)
notes: Checked against the original SEC EDGAR filing (SRC-0348), not the companiesmarketcap mirror (SRC-0537); wording identical, so no new source needed. Intel Foundry page also says EMIB 'In mass production since 2017'.

original_interpretation: Intel introduced EMIB-T in 2025 and expects its adoption to scale beginning in 2026; Intel says EMIB-T adds power delivery and bandwidth scalability for larger packages and next-generation memory.
evidence_found: "we introduced EMIB‑T in 2025, with adoption expected to scale beginning in 2026. EMIB‑T enhances the original EMIB technology by providing improved power delivery and bandwidth scalability to support larger package formats and next‑generation memory." (Intel FY2025 10-K, Packaging Technology)
notes: Verbatim match in SEC original. Adoption timing is Intel's expectation; reported_claim is correct.

original_interpretation: Intel targets Foveros-B and Foveros-R for high-volume manufacturing in 2027 and plans hybrid-bonding Foveros Direct on its Intel 18A-PT process in 2028.
evidence_found: "Foveros, ... which has expanded to include Foveros‑B and Foveros‑R, both targeted for high‑volume manufacturing in 2027" ... "Foveros Direct, announced in 2025, with hybrid‑bonding support planned on our Intel 18A‑PT process in 2028" (Intel FY2025 10-K, Packaging Technology)
notes: Verbatim match in SEC original. Targets, not achievements.

original_interpretation: In 2025 Intel's key assembly and test facilities were in China, New Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia; New Mexico was its key advanced packaging facility and a new advanced packaging facility was being built in Malaysia.
evidence_found: "In 2025, our key assembly and test facilities were in China, New Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia, with New Mexico being our key advanced packaging facility and a new advanced packaging facility being built in Malaysia." (Intel FY2025 10-K, Manufacturing, p.12)
notes: Verbatim match in SEC original. fact / company_filing is right.

original_interpretation: Intel's 10-K says disaggregated (chiplet) designs often need advanced substrates that are supply-constrained, and Intel expects industry-wide shortages of substrates, memory and other components may limit its ability to meet demand in 2026.
evidence_found: "a disaggregated approach often requires advanced substrates and other materials that can create additional manufacturing challenges when supply is constrained, as is the situation currently."; "We expect these supply constraints to persist into 2026 and industry wide shortages of substrates, memory and other critical components may further limit our ability to meet CCG and DCAI customer demand in 2026." (Intel FY2025 10-K, MD&A p.25)
notes: Both passages found in the SEC original. Risk language, correctly a reported_claim.

original_interpretation: In July 2026 TSMC's CEO said its packaging capacity was so tight that it was limiting customers' growth, and that he welcomed alternatives such as Intel's EMIB-T taking some of the load.
evidence_found: LSEG transcript: "our packaging capacity is so tight that now it limits my customers' growth. So we welcome that additional flexibility in the market" ... "we hope they will be successful and so that share some of the loading from TSMC." (answer to Macquarie's Arthur Lai on EMIB-T)
notes: Found in both the LSEG edited transcript on TSMC's IR site and the Motley Fool transcript ('now it's limiting'). Call date 16 July 2026.

original_interpretation: In July 2026 TSMC said it is building 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan over the next several years.
evidence_found: "At the same time, we are building 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan over the next several years, and we will continue to further invest in Taiwan." (TSMC 2Q26 call, CEO prepared remarks, LSEG transcript)
notes: Verbatim. No split between front-end and packaging fabs is given, as the metric population says.

original_interpretation: In July 2026 TSMC announced an additional US$100 billion Arizona investment for more 2 nm-and-below wafer fabs and advanced packaging fabs, bringing planned Arizona investment to US$265 billion, without a firm schedule.
evidence_found: CEO: "we would like to announce an additional USD100 billion investment in Arizona. This is to build several more semiconductor logic wafer fabs for 2-nanometer and below technologies, as well as advanced packaging fabs". Analyst: "now with total USD265 billion CapEx in Arizona"; IR restating: "So the total investment now is USD265 billion... Is that correct, Sunny?" CEO: "if you ask me to give you a firm schedule, no, we don't have it today"
notes: The US$100bn increment, its purpose and the lack of a firm schedule are stated by the CEO. The US$265bn total comes from the UBS analyst's question, restated by IR as a question; no executive states it, though nobody corrects it and it equals the earlier US$165bn plus US$100bn. LSEG transcript says USD; Motley Fool says 'TWD 265 billion' (transcription error). CEO also said 'probably additional four more fabs', front and back end combined (Fool).
correction: The US$265bn cumulative total was put forward by an analyst and restated by TSMC IR as a question; TSMC management did not state it outright.

original_interpretation: TSMC's CEO said front-end wafer and back-end packaging are different businesses, so gains by packaging competitors do not automatically threaten TSMC's wafer business ('If they are the same, you can expect ASE become the front-end competitor also').
evidence_found: C.C. Wei: "The front end's wafer business and the back end's business are two different things, right? If they are the same, you can expect ASE become the front-end competitor also. It's two different things." (Motley Fool transcript, answer to BofA's Haas Liu on whether EMIB-T is a gateway to front-end competition)
notes: Verbatim in the Motley Fool transcript. The question was explicitly whether packaging gains (EMIB-T) lead to front-end competition, so the paraphrase is fair. Not located in the truncated extract of the LSEG transcript.

original_interpretation: TSMC does not separate advanced packaging capex from testing, mask-making and other spending, and its CEO said money shifts between front-end and back-end bottleneck tools from year to year.
evidence_found: IR (Jeff Su): "when we guide for the CapEx, of course, we guide it in a bucket of packaging, testing, mask making, and others together." CFO (LSEG): "about 10% to 20% will be spent for advanced packaging, testing, mask making and others." CEO: "Sometimes we have a bottleneck, we put more money to buy the bottleneck tools, sometimes it's in the front end, sometimes it's in the back end."
notes: Bundled capex guidance and CEO's bottleneck comment are both supported. 'From year to year' is the researcher's addition: the CEO said 'sometimes' and gave no period. The CEO also called the back-end share 10%-20% long term.
correction: CEO said spending shifts 'sometimes' to wherever the bottleneck is; no year-to-year pattern was stated.

original_interpretation: In July 2026 TSMC said most of its advanced packaging is still CoWoS, that it is developing a lower-cost alternative with substrate vendors, and that the pilot line announced earlier needs about another year to mature before customer production.
evidence_found: LSEG: "today, the majority is still CoWoS, right? And we are developing that alternative, try to lower down the cost. And we also work with substrate vendor ... we're building a pipeline that I announced a few quarters ago, and it takes about another one year to be mature, so we can put into the production with our customer." Fool renders the same passage as "building a pilot line".
notes: Substance supported (answer to Citi's question on glass substrates/panel). The two transcripts disagree on the key noun: TSMC's own LSEG transcript says 'pipeline', Motley Fool says 'pilot line'. 'Pilot line' fits the context but rests on the third-party transcript.
correction: The 'pilot line' wording comes from the Motley Fool transcript; TSMC's LSEG transcript says 'pipeline'.

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2025 annual report lists seven Advanced Backend Fabs, all in Taiwan: AP1 Hsinchu, AP2 Tainan, AP3 Longtan (Taoyuan), AP5 Taichung, AP6 Zhunan (Miaoli), AP7 Chiayi and AP8 Tainan.
evidence_found: Contact Information lists "Advanced Backend Fab 1 ... Hsinchu"; "Advanced Backend Fab 2 ... Tainan"; "Advanced Backend Fab 3 ... Longtan Dist., Taoyuan"; "Advanced Backend Fab 5 ... Taichung"; "Advanced Backend Fab 6 ... Zhunan Township, Miaoli"; "Advanced Backend Fab 7 ... Taibao City, Chiayi County"; "Advanced Backend Fab 8 ... Xinshi Dist., Tainan City" (TSMC 2025 Annual Report, contact pages)
notes: Seven entries, no AP4, all in Taiwan. The report was printed 12 March 2026.

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2025 annual report says its expanded US investment plan includes three additional fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and a major R&D team center in Arizona.
evidence_found: "Also in 2025, TSMC announced its intention to expand its investment in advanced semiconductor manufacturing in the United States, including plans for three additional fabrication plants, two advanced packaging facilities and a major R&D team center." notes: Quote found. The sentence says 'in the United States' and does not name Arizona (preceding sentences are about TSMC Arizona). The plan was enlarged in July 2026 by a further US$100bn for more 2nm-and-below fabs and advanced packaging fabs (CLM-1577), so the three-fab/two-AP plan no longer describes TSMC's current US plan.
correction: The report says 'in the United States', not Arizona. The plan is superseded by the July 2026 expansion (additional US$100bn; CLM-1577).

original_interpretation: In April 2026 TSMC said it is producing 5.5-reticle-size CoWoS.
evidence_found: "The Company is now producing 5.5-reticle size CoWoS and planning for even larger versions." (TSMC press release, Santa Clara, 22 Apr 2026, 3DFabric section)
notes: Verbatim.

evidence_found: "A 14-reticle size CoWoS, capable of integrating approximately 10 large compute dies and 20 HBM stacks, is slated for production in 2028. This will be followed by an expansion to beyond 14 reticles in 2029." (TSMC press release, 22 Apr 2026)

original_interpretation: TSMC expects its 40-reticle-size SoW-X System-on-Wafer technology in 2029.

notes: Verbatim.

evidence_found: "with A14-to-A14 SoIC set to be available for production in 2029. It will provide 1.8X higher die-to-die I/O density compared with N2-on-N2 SoIC" (TSMC press release, 22 Apr 2026)
notes: Verbatim.

evidence_found: "a true co-packaged optics solution using COUPE on substrate beginning production in 2026. By integrating the COUPE optical engine directly inside the package, TSMC achieves 2X power efficiency and 10X latency reduction versus a pluggable version on the circuit board." (TSMC press release, 22 Apr 2026)

original_interpretation: TSMC describes InFO as a wafer-level fan-out integration technology with a high-density redistribution layer and through-InFO vias, offered in 2.5D and 3D options; its InFO-PoP has no organic substrate or C4 bump.
evidence_found: "Integrated Fan-Out (InFO) technology is an innovative wafer-level system integration technology featuring a high-density redistribution layer (RDL) and through-InFO vias (TIVs) ... InFO technology offers 2.5D and 3D options"; InFO-PoP "has better electrical and thermal performance, and a thinner profile than flip chip package-on-package, because it has no organic substrate or C4 bump." (TSMC InFO page)
notes: Verbatim.

original_interpretation: TSMC states it has shipped InFO in high volume since 2016.
evidence_found: "Production Milestone ... More than 20 product tape-outs are in production or in development as of Aug. 2019 ... TSMC has been shipping InFO in high volume since 2016" (TSMC 3DFabric InFO page, "Chronicle of InFO" timeline)
notes: The English page's timeline is script-loaded and did not render in the extractor (Cloudflare blocked the browser). The same 3dfabric.tsmc.com page in its simplified-Chinese site version carries the English sentence verbatim, and a search snippet of the English page shows the same text.

original_interpretation: Under an October 2024 MoU, TSMC will contract turnkey advanced packaging and test services from Amkor's planned Peoria, Arizona facility to serve customers of TSMC's Phoenix fabs, with technologies such as InFO and CoWoS to be jointly defined.

TSMC will leverage these services to support its customers, particularly those using TSMC's advanced wafer fabrication facilities in Phoenix." ... "The companies will jointly define the specific packaging technologies, such as TSMC's Integrated Fan-Out (InFO) and Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS®)" (joint release, 4 Oct 2024)
notes: Verbatim. The agreement is a memorandum of understanding, as the claim says.

original_interpretation: Intel describes EMIB as a silicon bridge embedded in the package substrate; EMIB-M adds MIM capacitors in the bridge and EMIB-T adds through-silicon vias to the bridge.
evidence_found: "EMIB-M features MIM capacitors in the bridge. EMIB-T adds TSVs to the bridge. Silicon bridge embedded in package substrate for shoreline-to-shoreline connection." (Intel Foundry packaging page, EMIB 2.5D)
notes: Verbatim (rendered with the browser).

original_interpretation: Intel describes Foveros-S as a 2.5D silicon interposer of up to 4x reticle in mass production since 2019, Foveros-R as an RDL-interposer option production-ready in 2027, and Foveros Direct as Cu-to-Cu hybrid-bonded 3D stacking on an active base die.
evidence_found: Foveros-S: "Silicon interposer with 4x reticle." "Production proven: In mass production since 2019 with active base die." Foveros-R: "Features a redistribution layer (RDL) interposer" "Production ready in 2027." Foveros Direct 3D: "3D stacking of chiplets on active base die" "Cu-to-Cu hybrid bonding interface (HBI)." (Intel Foundry packaging page)
notes: All elements found. Minor: the page says 'with 4x reticle', not 'up to'. Foveros-R's 2027 date matches the 10-K (CLM-1561).

original_interpretation: At Direct Connect in April 2025 Intel said Intel 18A-PT can connect to top dies through Foveros Direct with a hybrid-bonding interconnect pitch below 5 µm, launched EMIB-T, and announced a new engagement with Amkor on advanced packaging.
evidence_found: "Intel 18A-PT can be connected to top die using Foveros Direct 3D with hybrid bonding interconnect pitch less than 5 micrometers (µm)."; "New advanced packaging technology offerings include EMIB-T to enable future high bandwidth memory needs"; "A new engagement with Amkor Technology increases customer flexibility" (Intel press release, 29 Apr 2025)
notes: Verbatim.

original_interpretation: Samsung Foundry offers 2.5D I-Cube in two variants: I-CubeS on a silicon interposer and I-CubeE, which embeds silicon bridges in a TSV-less fan-out panel-level RDL interposer; H-Cube combines fine-pattern ABF and HDI substrates for larger I-Cube packages.
evidence_found: "I-Cube is available in I-CubeS and I-CubeE derivatives based on the interposer type." "I-CubeE has silicon embedded structure which covers advantages of both silicon bridge by fine patterning and RDL interposer with TSV-less structure and large interposer size by applying FO-PLP, i.e., fan-out panel level package." "H-Cube is ... the combination of fine patterning ABF ... substrate and HDI ... substrate which allows large size into I-Cube 2.5D packaging." (Samsung AHI page)
notes: I-CubeE and H-Cube descriptions match. The page does not explicitly say I-CubeS uses a silicon interposer. It only says the variants differ by interposer type and that I-CubeE 'gets more cost-effective over a silicon interposer'. That I-CubeS is silicon is implied, not stated.
correction: The page does not explicitly say I-CubeS uses a silicon interposer; this is implied.

original_interpretation: Samsung Foundry's 3D X-Cube comes in micro-bump and hybrid-copper-bonding versions, and Samsung says it is developing Cu-Cu connections at pitches below 4 µm.
evidence_found: "X-Cube (u-Bump)"; "X-Cube (Hybrid Copper Bonding) ... HCB (Hybrid Copper Bonding): The hybrid Cu-Cu connections have a lot of advantages ... Samsung Foundry is in progress of developing the ultra-fine pitch Cu-Cu connections such as less than 4um." (Samsung AHI page)
notes: Verbatim.

original_interpretation: ASE said in July 2026 that its 2026 leading-edge advanced packaging (LEAP) services revenue was tracking ahead of its prior US$3.5 billion guidance and that it aims to double LEAP revenue in 2027.
evidence_found: "For full year, LEAP services revenue is tracking ahead of prior guidance of US$3.5 billion" (ASE 2Q26 earnings release, 30 Jul 2026, p.3); CFO Joseph Tung: "this year's LEAP service revenue tracking ahead of our prior quarter guidance of USD 3.5 billion ... we are aiming to double our LEAP revenue in 2027." (Q2 2026 call)
notes: Release text checked directly; the 2027 aim checked in the Motley Fool transcript. The 'prior guidance' of US$3.5bn was set in April 2026 (Taipei Times: up from US$3.2bn).

original_interpretation: In Q2 2026 bump, flip chip, wafer-level packaging and SiP made up 49% of ASE's ATM revenue by type, versus 24% for wire bonding and 19% for testing.
evidence_found: "ATM Revenues by Type" chart (p.10), Q2/26 column in PDF text layer: 49% (Bump/FC/WLP/SiP), 24% (Wirebonding), 6% (Others), 19% (Testing), 2% (Material). Cross-check p.7 ATM P&L: Testing NT$23,665m of NT$126,148m = 18.8%; Packaging 79.5% ≈ 49+24+6.
notes: Chart values read from the PDF text layer. Series labels were assigned by size and confirmed against the ATM income statement (testing 18.8%, packaging 79.5%). fact / investor_presentation is acceptable for company segment data.

original_interpretation: ASE raised 2026 capex to about US$10.5 billion: US$4 billion for buildings and facilities and US$6.5 billion for equipment, with about 70% of equipment capex for leading-edge.
evidence_found: CFO Joseph Tung: "this year, we're raising the CapEx by another $2 billion. That brings up the total to about $10.5 billion. And out of this $10.5 billion, $4 billion will be for new factory buildings and facilities and $6.5 billion for equipment" ... "for equipment, I think it's about 56% is for assembly, 40% for test ... I think 70% of the equipment CapEx is for leading edge for this year." (ASE Q2 2026 call, Motley Fool)
notes: Verbatim. Matches the trail: US$7bn in Feb, +US$1.5bn in Apr (Taipei Times), +US$2bn in Jul. Only a third-party transcript is the source; the earnings release gives just the 1H26 capex actuals.

original_interpretation: ASE said it has 13 greenfield and 8 brownfield factory projects under way, which it expects to carry its capacity needs into 2028 and part of 2029.
evidence_found: CFO: "at this very moment, we are having 13 greenfield projects going on. We have another 8 brownfield projects. brownfield -- by brownfield, we mean that we are acquiring existing factories and trying to renovate them ... I think the current projects will be sufficient for us to carry ourselves into '28 and maybe into some part of '29." (ASE Q2 2026 call, Motley Fool)
notes: Verbatim.

original_interpretation: ASE said its capacity was close to full in 2Q26 (blended utilisation 80-85%) and that near-term growth was gated by its ability to install equipment and build out buildings and facilities.
evidence_found: IR head Kenneth Hsiang: "Effectively, outside of equipment lines being placed into service, capacities were generally very close to being full. Our blended utilization rate for the quarter was between 80% to 85%. Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities." (ASE Q2 2026 call, Motley Fool)
notes: Verbatim, with the speaker confirmed.

original_interpretation: ASE said its fully automated 310 mm x 310 mm panel-level packaging line will start production by Q1 2027 and that it will not have glass substrates in production within the next 12 months.
evidence_found: Tien Wu: "our fully automated line will start production by Q1 of next year. And that is in the form factor of 310 by 310." ... "right now, we do not have the glass substrate in production, not for the next 12 months, if that's the question you're asking." (ASE Q2 2026 call, Motley Fool)
notes: Verbatim. 'Next year' = 2027 (call held 30 Jul 2026).

original_interpretation: ASE said it also works with customers on Intel's EMIB and sees no conflict as a pure-play OSAT: if EMIB substrates become an alternative, ASE would do the assembly.
evidence_found: Tien Wu: "For ASE, we're also collaborating with the other customers also along the same line, including EMIB." ... "I don't think there's a potential threat. Again, we are a pure-play. If the EMIB substrate becomes the right alternative, which is by EMIB substrate, and we do the assembly, there is no conflict." (ASE Q2 2026 call, Motley Fool)
notes: Verbatim. Context: Wu also said 'our focus is to support the CoWoS'.

original_interpretation: ASE expects about 300 million of 2026 revenue from 'full-process' CoWoS-like packaging (doing all steps rather than only the on-substrate step), with substantial growth in 2027.
evidence_found: Q1 call (CFO Joseph Tung): "we still believe that we can reach this TWD 300 million dollar revenue mark this for this year." Q2 call: "this year, we said that we're going to have about TWD 300 million worth of revenue coming from that space, and things are on track." Taipei Times, 30 Apr 2026: "full-process LEAP services, a business that is projected to generate US$300 million in revenue this year, Tung said."
notes: The figure, the 2026 period and the 2027 growth outlook are supported. The currency can now be settled: the Taipei Times staff report on the call gives US$300 million. The transcripts' 'TWD ... million dollar' is self-contradictory, and NT$300m (~US$9m) would be implausible next to US$3.5bn of LEAP revenue. The Taipei Times is tier 3, so the USD reading is well supported but not from a primary document.
correction: Currency is USD: full-process LEAP revenue was guided at about US$300 million for 2026 (Taipei Times report of CFO Tung). See the superseding claim.

original_interpretation: ASE said its LEAP revenue is about 75% assembly and 25% test, and within test about 75% wafer sort and 25% final test.
evidence_found: CFO Joseph Tung: "In terms of combination, I think it's about 75% in assembly and 25% in tests. With tests, we have about 75% in wafer sort and 25% in final tests." (ASE Q1 2026 call, StockAnalysis transcript)
notes: Verbatim, with the speaker confirmed. Only an aggregator transcript (tier 3) is the source; the split is an approximation.

original_interpretation: ASE said its LEAP lines must be installed at scale as a full set of different machines, so they take longer to bring up and tune than traditional lines, and depreciation rises before revenue during qualification.
evidence_found: IR head Kenneth Hsiang: "Our LEAP lines must be installed at scale and together as a full set of differing machinery instead of in small incremental units like wire bonders and testers. This results in our LEAP lines taking a greater amount of time to bring up and tune ... we will continue to see gradually increasing depreciation without significant amounts of associated revenue during the tuning and qualification period." (ASE Q1 2026 call)
notes: Verbatim, with the speaker confirmed. Applies to OS and full-process LEAP lines being tuned in 1H26.

original_interpretation: Amkor's 'advanced products' (flip chip, memory, wafer-level processing and related test) were US$1,557 million of its US$1,898 million Q2 2026 net sales (about 82%).

evidence_found: Business Outlook: "Full year 2026 capital expenditures of approximately $2.5 billion to $3.0 billion" (Amkor 8-K Ex. 99.1, 27 Jul 2026)
notes: Verbatim in the SEC original. This is guidance.

original_interpretation: Besi reported that by end-2025 cumulative hybrid-bonding orders since 2021 exceeded 150 systems from 18 customers, and that six integrated hybrid-bonding lines with 30 Besi bonders were installed at a leading logic customer together with Applied Materials.
evidence_found: FY2025 release (19 Feb 2026), CEO comment: "hybrid bonding adoption expanded to 18 customers, cumulative orders grew to 150+ systems ... six integrated hybrid bonding production lines were installed at a leading logic customer incorporating 30 Besi hybrid bonders in collaboration with Applied Materials." Q2-26 release (23 Jul 2026): "Hybrid bonding customer adoption increased from 15 at year end 2025 to 21 at the end of Q2-26".

Besi's own Q2-26 release later put end-2025 hybrid-bonding customers at 15, not 18; recorded as a contradiction. Unexplained, possibly a changed definition.
correction: Drop 'since 2021' (not in the source). Besi's July 2026 release restates end-2025 hybrid-bonding customers as 15, not 18.
